title: Episode 304: The Black Prince and Richard II: The Triumph of Poitiers, the Peasants' Revolt, and the Deposition
description:
The dramatic tale of Edward the Black Prince and his doomed son, King Richard II. Edward of Woodstock was the invincible warrior-prince who captured the King of France at Poitiers in 1356. His premature death left the crown to ten-year-old Richard II. When the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 engulfed London, the fourteen-year-old boy king faced down Wat Tyler's furious mob at Smithfield with breathtaking courage. Yet Richard's belief in the divine, untrammeled power of monarchy ignited ferocious conflict with his nobility, the Lords Appellant, and his ambitious cousin Henry Bolingbroke. Deposed in 1399 and murdered in Pontefract Castle, Richard's fall brought a tragic end to three centuries of direct Plantagenet rule. Discover the boy king and the warrior prince.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series explores one of the most dramatic chapters in medieval history: the brilliant military glory of Edward the Black Prince, and the tempestuous, tragic reign of his son, King Richard II. Here is George with the gripping story of the boy king, Wat Tyler's rebellion, and the fall of the Plantagenets.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE CHIVALRIC HERO: EDWARD OF WOODSTOCK AT POITIERS AND NÁJERA
Edward of Woodstock, known to posterity as the Black Prince—perhaps from the black embossed armor he wore at tournaments, or the dark terror he struck into French hearts—was the quintessential chivalric hero of fourteenth-century Europe. Eldest son of Edward III, he won his spurs at sixteen commanding the van at Crécy. Ten years later, in September 1356, commanding an army of barely seven thousand men near Poitiers, he was intercepted by King John II of France with twenty thousand elite troops. Utilizing marshy terrain, vineyard hedges, and deadly longbow crossfire, the Black Prince routed the French cavalry. In a climactic melee, King John II and his young son were captured alive. The Black Prince treated the captive French monarch with legendary chivalric courtesy, personally serving him wine at dinner in his royal pavilion and refusing to sit in his presence as an equal. Created Prince of Aquitaine, he established a dazzling court at Bordeaux. In 1367, he led an army across the frozen Pyrenees to restore Pedro the Cruel to the throne of Castile, achieving another masterclass tactical victory at Nájera. But the Spanish campaign proved his undoing: he contracted an incurable, debilitating dysentery and malarial fever that broke his iron health, draining his finances and forcing his return to England in 1371 as a dying shadow of the great warrior he once was. At the height of his powers in Aquitaine, the Black Prince held one of the most extravagant and cultured courts in Europe, where the finest troubadours, armorers, and falconers gathered. Yet his iron determination could shade into terrifying brutality: when the French city of Limoges rebelled against his taxation in 1370, the bedridden prince was carried into the breach on a litter, ordering the summary slaughter of over three thousand citizens, an act of merciless fury that stained his chivalric reputation forever.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE BOY KING AND THE SPARK OF 1381: THE POLL TAX
When the Black Prince died in June 1376, England wept for its fallen champion. Just twelve months later, King Edward III died, leaving the crown to the Black Prince's only surviving son, Richard of Bordeaux, a handsome, golden-haired boy of just ten years. Crowned Richard II at Westminster in a ceremony of unprecedented theatrical splendor, the child monarch was carried on the shoulders of his knights after the four-hour service, having lost one of his coronation slippers in the throng. Governance fell to a council dominated by his immensely wealthy and unpopular uncle, John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster. Decades of continuous warfare with France had drained the royal treasury, while French coastal raids plundered English ports from Rye to Plymouth. To finance the war, Parliament enacted three successive and regressive Poll Taxes between 1377 and 1381, taxing every man and woman over fourteen years of age regardless of wealth. For a peasantry already bearing the burdens of feudal servitude and legally capped wages following the Black Death, the third poll tax of 1381, levied at an extortionate twelve pence per person, was the breaking point. When royal tax commissioners arrived in Essex and Kent to inspect registers and enforce collection, furious villagers drove them out with pitchforks and scythes, igniting the largest social rebellion in medieval English history. The anger against the poll tax of 1381 was intensified by widespread corruption among the tax collectors, who reportedly subjected young village girls to degrading physical examinations to verify whether they were over the age of fourteen. When John Bampton, a royal commissioner, arrived at Brentwood in Essex to enforce collection, local fishermen and farmers flatly refused to pay a single penny, chasing the commissioner and his armed men into the woods and sparking the flames of insurrection across southern England.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE PEASANTS' REVOLT: WAT TYLER, JOHN BALL, AND THE TOWER
Under the charismatic leadership of Wat Tyler, an experienced soldier from Kent, and the radical, fiery preaching of the itinerant priest John Ball—who famously asked, 'When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?'—tens of thousands of armed peasants marched on London in June 1381. Demanding the total abolition of serfdom, the repeal of all labor statutes, and the confiscation of church wealth, the rebels swarmed the city gates. Sympathetic London apprentices and artisans flung open the gates of Aldgate and London Bridge, welcoming the insurgents into the heart of the capital. London descended into chaos: the rebels sacked and burned John of Gaunt's magnificent Savoy Palace, throwing barrels of gunpowder into the flames and dumping his treasures into the River Thames, declaring they were seekers of justice, not common thieves. They stormed the Fleet Prison and beheaded Flemish merchants in the streets. Fourteen-year-old King Richard, along with his ministers and the royal court, took refuge in the formidable stone fortress of the Tower of London. But while Richard was away attempting to negotiate with rebel factions at Mile End, insurgents broke directly into the Tower. They dragged Archbishop of Canterbury Simon Sudbury and Royal Treasurer Sir Robert Hales out to Tower Hill and brutally beheaded them on a log, parading their severed heads on pikes across London Bridge. The sacking of the Savoy Palace was an act of disciplined fury: the rebels threw John of Gaunt's gold plate and silk tapestries into the Thames, and when one looter attempted to conceal a silver cup in his tunic, the mob threw him into the flames alongside the treasures, shouting that they were men of truth and justice, not common thieves. Archbishop Sudbury was dragged to Tower Hill while celebrating mass, and his execution was so botched that it took eight clumsy blows of an ax to sever his head.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE CONFRONTATION AT SMITHFIELD: 'I WILL BE YOUR LEADER!'
On Saturday, June 15, 1381, the teenage king rode out to Smithfield market outside the city walls to meet Wat Tyler and thirty thousand armed insurgents. Tyler rode forward alone on a little horse to confront the king, treating the monarch with insolent familiarity, shaking his hand, rinsing his mouth with water, and demanding that all men be made equal under the king with all noble titles abolished. During the tense negotiation, an altercation erupted between Tyler and the royal retinue. Sir William Walworth, the fiercely loyal Mayor of London, stepped forward, drew a baselard dagger, and slashed Tyler across the throat, while another royal squire ran him through with a sword. Tyler slumped mortally wounded onto the cobblestones. The rebel crowd saw their fallen general, notched their longbows, and shouted, 'Treason! They have slain our captain! Let us kill them all!' At that fateful second, fourteen-year-old King Richard spurred his horse forward into the open field directly toward the angry mob. Holding up his hand, his clear boyish voice rang out: 'Sirs, will you shoot your king? I am your captain and your leader! Follow me into the field, and you shall have all that you desire!' Mesmerized by his courage and royal majesty, the rebels lowered their weapons and followed Richard into St. John's Fields. Walworth quickly gathered thousands of armed London citizens, encircling the rebels. The uprising was broken. Weeks later, when peasants presented their charters for confirmation, Richard revoked every concession, declaring with cold fury: 'Serfs you are, and serfs you shall remain.' Walworth's strike against Wat Tyler was motivated by Tyler's insolent posture: the rebel chief had spat beer upon the cobblestones before the king's horse and fingered the hilt of his dagger. Richard's instinctive courage at that knife-edge moment saved the monarchy: by riding straight into the path of twenty thousand drawn longbows, the fourteen-year-old sovereign disarmed their wrath with royal charisma, demonstrating an innate, majestic presence that made the peasants believe the King was truly their friend against the greedy barons.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE LORDS APPELLANT AND THE MERCILESS PARLIAMENT: 1386 TO 1388
Richard's triumph at Smithfield forged in the young king an absolute, almost mystical belief in the divine, untrammeled prerogative of the royal crown. As he reached adulthood, Richard cultivated an opulent, refined court centered on literature, fashion, and haute cuisine—introducing the handkerchief and patronizing poets like Geoffrey Chaucer. But his lavish favoritism toward corrupt courtiers, particularly his close favorite Robert de Vere, Earl of Oxford, enraged England's traditional warrior nobility. In 1386, five powerful magnates—known as the Lords Appellant, including Richard's uncle the Duke of Gloucester and his cousin Henry Bolingbroke—rose in armed rebellion against royal favorites. De Vere's royalist army was routed at the Battle of Radcot Bridge in December 1387, and de Vere fled into continental exile. In February 1388, the triumphant Lords Appellant summoned the 'Merciless Parliament' at Westminster. Stripping the young king of all governing power, the parliament impeached and executed Richard's closest friends and tutors, including Sir Simon de Burley, the venerable knight who had negotiated his marriage. Richard, forced to sign the death warrants while his queen pleaded on her knees in vain, never forgot or forgave the humiliation, locking his bitter hatred away behind a mask of courteous obedience. Richard's court introduced Italianate fashions, pointed poulaine shoes stuffed with moss, and the delicate cultural refinements that rough English barons despised as effeminate extravagance. When the Merciless Parliament condemned Sir Simon de Burley, Queen Anne of Bohemia fell to her knees before the Earl of Arundel, weeping for hours to beg for his life, but Arundel coldly told her that she had better pray for herself and her husband, an insult Richard never forgot or forgave.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: AUTOCRACY, VENGEANCE, AND THE EXILE OF HENRY BOLINGBROKE: 1397 TO 1399
For nearly a decade, Richard governed with apparent moderation, waiting patiently for the moment to strike. By 1397, having negotiated a peace treaty with France and secured a loyal personal bodyguard of seven hundred Welsh and Cheshire archers who guarded him day and night, Richard sprang his trap. The leading Lords Appellant were arrested in swift nocturnal raids: the Duke of Gloucester was smothered to death with a feather bed in prison at Calais, the Earl of Arundel was publicly beheaded, and the Earl of Warwick was exiled to the Isle of Man. Richard declared himself an absolute monarch above the law, demanding that courtiers bow to the floor whenever his royal gaze fell upon them. In 1398, an escalating quarrel between the two surviving Appellants, Henry Bolingbroke and Thomas Mowbray, was scheduled to be settled by judicial duel at Coventry. Just as the two armored knights lowered their lances and spurred their warhorses toward each other, Richard dramatically threw down his royal baton, stopping the combat and exiling both men—Mowbray for life, and Bolingbroke for ten years. When Bolingbroke's father, John of Gaunt, died in February 1399, Richard made his fatal error: he disinherited Bolingbroke, confiscating the vast Duchy of Lancaster to the Crown, terrifying every landowning noble in England that their inheritances were no longer safe. Richard surrounded himself with a private army of Cheshire archers wearing his personal badge of the White Hart, men who guarded him during Parliament with notched arrows aimed at the benches of the Commons. His confiscation of the Lancastrian patrimony following John of Gaunt's death violated the fundamental feudal contract: if the King could arbitrarily strip the greatest noble house of its ancestral estates, no lord, knight, or yeoman in England was secure in his inheritance.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE DEPOSITION AT FLINT CASTLE AND THE TRAGEDY OF PONTEFRACT
In May 1399, confident in his absolute supremacy, Richard sailed for Ireland with his royal army to suppress native rebellions. In July, Henry Bolingbroke landed at Ravenspur in Yorkshire with just sixty exiled men, declaring he had returned only to claim his rightful inheritance as Duke of Lancaster. Within weeks, nobles, gentry, and common soldiers rallied to Bolingbroke by the tens of thousands. When Richard returned across the Irish Sea in August, his army melted away in the Welsh hills. Trapped at Flint Castle, Richard looked down from the battlements to see Bolingbroke's massive host surrounding the fortress. Weeping bitter tears, Richard surrendered, being led captive to London on an emaciated horse while the crowds cheered Bolingbroke. In September 1399, assembled at Westminster Hall beneath the magnificent hammerbeam roof Richard had commissioned, Parliament read thirty-three articles of deposition against the king. Richard formally renounced the crown, sobbing as he placed the regalia in Bolingbroke's hands, who claimed the throne as King Henry IV. Imprisoned in the dark dungeons of Pontefract Castle in Yorkshire, Richard II was starved to death in early 1400 at age thirty-three, or murdered by his jailers. His tragic deposition severed the direct Plantagenet line, igniting the dynastic curse that would culminate in the Wars of the Roses. At Flint Castle, Richard reportedly stood upon the high tower gazing out toward the Dee estuary, saying to the Earl of Salisbury: 'Fair cousin, I see our ruin is at hand; for the love of God, take heed to your life.' In his cold stone chamber at Pontefract, Richard met his end in total obscurity; whether starved to death or bludgeoned by assassins, his body was displayed publicly at St. Paul's Cathedral with only his face visible, proving to the skeptical realm that the last direct Plantagenet was truly dead.
